1. INTRODUCTION
As the manufacture of integrated circuits advances toward
smaller sizes and higher integration densities, the requirements
for interconnect materials are becoming more stringent, while
the limitations of traditional copper interconnection have
become increasingly apparent.<sup>1−6</sup> The resistivity of copper
interconnects increases exponentially when the width falls
below the copper mean free path, primarily due to frequent
electron scattering at interfaces and grain boundaries, which
becomes the main factor determining the resistivity.<sup>7,8</sup> In
contrast, cobalt interconnects possess better properties, such as
very short electronic mean free path, relatively low price, and
good compatibility in silicon-based electronic chips.<sup>9−11</sup>
Besides, cobalt has a higher melting point, which is more
beneficial to reduce the electromigration caused by atomic
difusion.<sup>12</sup> These properties are particularly beneficial for
applications in advanced integrated circuit assemblies in the
post-Moore’s law era. Therefore, cobalt is expected to be a new
generation of interconnection material instead of traditional
copper.
The manufacture process of cobalt interconnects is similar to
that of copper interconnects and is compatible with existing
electrodeposition processes for copper damascene intercon-
nects. The electrodeposition process for cobalt interconnection
is an advanced interconnect technology for integrated circuits
that utilizes a wet electrochemical deposition method to
bottom-up fill the interconnect structures of semiconductor
chips with cobalt metal. Electrodeposition has the advantages
of simple operation, easy control of process parameters, and
low cost and is considered to be the main technology for cobalt
filling at present.<sup>16−18</sup> In recent years, the process of copper
electrodeposition has been thoroughly studied, leading to a
comprehensive understanding of the bottom-up electro
deposition (superfilling) mechanism, which is also applied to
cobalt electrodeposition to achieve defect-free interconnect
structures.<sup>19,20</sup>
The search for suitable additives is the core to fulfill the
bottom-up electrodeposition mechanism. Generally, the
electrodeposition rate of cobalt changes in diferent positions
of the hole due to changing thermodynamics across the
additive concentration gradient.<sup>21,22</sup> When the deposition rate
at the bottom of the hole is higher than that at the upper part
of the hole, it can obtain the void-free superfilling deposition of
cobalt in the microvias, holes, or trenches from bottom to
to
p.<sup>23−25</sup> These additives have efects on controlling the
deposition process and have influence on the surface
morphology, crystal structure, and electrical properties of the
cobalt films.<sup>26−29</sup> The research on cobalt electroplating
additives has focused on finding compounds that can achieve
superfilling while improving plating properties. However, there
are few reports and research studies in this field, particularly for
the superfilling processes at present.

1. INTRODUCTION
As the manufacture of integrated circuits advances toward
smaller sizes and higher integration densities, the requirements
for interconnect materials are becoming more stringent, while
the limitations of traditional copper interconnection have
become increasingly apparent.<sup>1−6</sup> The resistivity of copper
interconnects increases exponentially when the width falls
below the copper mean free path, primarily due to frequent
electron scattering at interfaces and grain boundaries, which
becomes the main factor determining the resistivity.<sup>7,8</sup> In
contrast, cobalt interconnects possess better properties, such as
very short electronic mean free path, relatively low price, and
good compatibility in silicon-based electronic chips.<sup>9−11</sup>
Besides, cobalt has a higher melting point, which is more
beneficial to reduce the electromigration caused by atomic
difusion.<sup>12</sup> These properties are particularly beneficial for
applications in advanced integrated circuit assemblies in the
post-Moore’s law era. Therefore, cobalt is expected to be a new
generation of interconnection material instead of traditional
copper.
The manufacture process of cobalt interconnects is similar to
that of copper interconnects and is compatible with existing
electrodeposition processes for copper damascene intercon-
nects. The electrodeposition process for cobalt interconnection
is an advanced interconnect technology for integrated circuits
that utilizes a wet electrochemical deposition method to
bottom-up fill the interconnect structures of semiconductor
chips with cobalt metal. Electrodeposition has the advantages
of simple operation, easy control of process parameters, and
low cost and is considered to be the main technology for cobalt
filling at present.<sup>16−18</sup> In recent years, the process of copper
electrodeposition has been thoroughly studied, leading to a
comprehensive understanding of the bottom-up electro
deposition (superfilling) mechanism, which is also applied to
cobalt electrodeposition to achieve defect-free interconnect
structures.<sup>19,20</sup>
The search for suitable additives is the core to fulfill the
bottom-up electrodeposition mechanism. Generally, the
electrodeposition rate of cobalt changes in diferent positions
of the hole due to changing thermodynamics across the
additive concentration gradient.<sup>21,22</sup> When the deposition rate
at the bottom of the hole is higher than that at the upper part
of the hole, it can obtain the void-free superfilling deposition of
cobalt in the microvias, holes, or trenches from bottom to
to
p.<sup>23−25</sup> These additives have efects on controlling the
deposition process and have influence on the surface
morphology, crystal structure, and electrical properties of the
cobalt films.<sup>26−29</sup> The research on cobalt electroplating
additives has focused on finding compounds that can achieve
superfilling while improving plating properties. However, there
are few reports and research studies in this field, particularly for
the superfilling processes at present.
In this work, we propose a cobalt electrodeposition additive
which can be used for superfilling. The inhibition efect of
alkyne-PEG4-amine (AP4A) was investigated by electro-
chemical methods, including cyclic voltammetry and chro-
nopotentiometry. Quantum chemical calculations were applied
to confirm the inhibition efect of the AP4A molecule on
electrodeposition. The results of the cobalt electrodeposition
experiment showed that AP4A has significant influence on
electrical properties, surface morphology, and crystal structure.
In superfilling of nanometer scale structures with high aspect
ratios, the additive AP4A was used to achieve bottom-up cobalt
electrodeposition successfully. This study provides a targeted
solution for superfilled cobalt plating, which has a good role in
promoting the development of electroplating in the future.

To assess the electrical performance of the cobalt films,

samples. The additive-free cobalt film demonstrates the lowest
resistivity, approximately 10.2 μΩ·cm. After the addition of
AP4A, the resistivity remains low and stabilizes at around 11−
12 μΩ·cm. The resistivity slightly increases as the concen-
tration of AP4A increases, which may be attributed to the
nonmetallic impurities added by additive doping in the
electrodeposition process. The impurity distribution in cobalt
films with and without 5 ppm AP4A was investigated by TOF-
SIMS (Figure 4c,d). It is obvious that the content of some
organic impurity elements (especially N) are increased, while
the N element only originates from the additive AP4A,
confirming the introduction of nonmetallic impurities by the
additive.
3.4. Cobalt Superfilling. In the electrodeposition process,
the constraints of the hole geometry lead to higher electric field
and mass-transport conditions at the top of the hole.<sup>36,37</sup> The
current and ion concentration at the top of the hole is often
higher than at the bottom; as a result, cobalt tends to deposit
more rapidly at the top than at the bottom, resulting in the
formation of structures containing voids. Besides, as the
current density increases, the possibility of void formation also
rises, which is attributed to a more pronounced concentration
of current at the top of the hole and an increased restriction on
mass-transport at the bottom. Therefore, in terms of current
parameter settings, the electrodeposition was carried out using
segmental currents and starting from a small current (Table 2)
in order to optimize the filling process, improve the filling
eficiency, and reduce the defects (such as pores and voids) in
the process.

spans.content: Based on the above study, cobalt superfilling electro-
deposition was performed with AP4A. The cross-sectional
view (Figure 5) confirms AP4A’s capability as an inhibitor in
cobalt superfilling. In this work, the concentration of AP4A is 5
ppm, which achieved bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition. The
bottom-up filling mechanism is depicted in Figure 6. During
the process of cobalt electrodeposition, AP4A molecules are
adsorbed on the surface of the electrode, modulating the
partial electric field strength and current density distribution.
In addition, under the influence of mass transport, the
molecules have a higher concentration at the top of the hole,
leading to a more significant inhibitory efect and slowing
down the rate of reduction of the cobalt ions. As a result, the
electric field and concentration gradient developed in the
presence of the AP4A molecules lead to a higher rate of
deposition of cobalt ions at the bottom of the hole than at the
top, resulting in the expected bottom-up superfilling.

deposition was performed with AP4A. The cross-sectional
view (Figure 5) confirms AP4A’s capability as an inhibitor in
cobalt superfilling. In this work, the concentration of AP4A is 5
ppm, which achieved bottom-up cobalt electrodeposition. The
bottom-up filling mechanism is depicted in Figure 6. During
the process of cobalt electrodeposition, AP4A molecules are
adsorbed on the surface of the electrode, modulating the
partial electric field strength and current density distribution.
In addition, under the influence of mass transport, the
molecules have a higher concentration at the top of the hole,
leading to a more significant inhibitory efect and slowing
down the rate of reduction of the cobalt ions. As a result, the
electric field and concentration gradient developed in the
presence of the AP4A molecules lead to a higher rate of
deposition of cobalt ions at the bottom of the hole than at the
top, resulting in the expected bottom-up superfilling.
4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, this research successfully achieved cobalt
superfilling in high aspect ratio nanometer scale structures
under the action of AP4A. From the analysis of electrochemical
tests and quantum chemical calculations, the cobalt electro
deposition inhibitor AP4A shows a splendid ability for
polarization, mainly resulting from the capacity for donating
electrons of the amino group. Furthermore, AP4A can afect
the surface morphology and crystalline structure of the cobalt
film. Under the efect of AP4A, the cobalt film maintains
excellent electrical properties while obtaining better flatness

In this work, the feasibility for achieving superfilling with
additives is assessed by electrochemical experiments and
quantum chemical calculations in the first place, which is
verified by practical filling of electrodeposition. This research
successfully identifies an additive molecule that can be used for
cobalt superfilling and investigates its inhibition mechanism as
well as its film properties, providing helpful insights into the
relationship between molecule and microstructure, which is
meaningful for realizing high-quality nanoscale cobalt inter
connections and for the search of other potential additives.
